issues.legal_issue: Government control powers do not authorize taking exclusive possession of an undertaking and its assets when the governing laws authorize control for specified public purposes.
material_facts: The undertaking had been closed before the State Government appointed a controller under the industrial disputes law.
The State and Central Government orders placed the undertaking in the controller’s exclusive possession and authorized him to dispose of its funds and property.
The Attorney General conceded that neither order was warranted by the law under which it purported to have been made.
issues.conclusion: Both government orders were invalid and were set aside and quashed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(f) of the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and Section 3(4) of the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1946 authorized specified functions of control for their respective statutory purposes; they did not warrant orders taking exclusive possession of the undertaking and conferring power to dispose of its assets. The Court also observed that the later amendments to the U.P. Act could not validate an order of a kind not contemplated by the original authority. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.writ_challenged_government_control_order: A person brought a constitutional writ challenging government orders appointing a controller over an undertaking.
predicates.undertaking_had_closed_before_the_orders: The undertaking had ceased operating before the challenged control orders were made.
predicates.orders_conferred_exclusive_possession_an: The government orders gave the controller exclusive possession of the undertaking and authority to dispose of its assets.
predicates.enabling_laws_authorized_control_for_spe: The laws under which the orders were made authorized control functions for specified public purposes.

issues.definition: When a writ challenges control orders made after an undertaking has closed, and those orders grant exclusive possession and asset-disposal powers beyond the control authorized for specified public purposes, the orders are invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A deprivation of property that began before the Constitution and continues after it may be challenged under Article 32 because its continuing operation conflicts with the fundamental rights protected by the Constitution.
material_facts: The State Government’s order taking control of the undertaking was made before the Constitution came into force.
A later Central Government order was relied on to retain possession after the Constitution came into force.
The petitioner claimed that the continuing deprivation of property violated Article 31 and sought relief under Article 32.
issues.conclusion: The petition was maintainable under Article 32; the continuing deprivation came into conflict with the fundamental rights when the Constitution came into force and became void from then under Article 13(1).
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 31 and 32, a continuing deprivation of property could be challenged even if it began before the Constitution came into force. By Article 13(1), an existing measure that continued to conflict with fundamental rights became void from the Constitution’s commencement. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.constitutional_writ_petition: A person brought a constitutional writ petition seeking relief from government action.
predicates.property_deprivation_continued_after_con: A deprivation of property that had begun earlier continued after constitutional protections became operative.
predicates.continuing_possession_was_supported_by_a: The government relied on an order to continue holding the property.

issues.definition: When a constitutional writ petition concerns a government-supported property deprivation that continues after constitutional protections begin, the continuing deprivation is challengeable under constitutional writ jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: After invalid government orders taking an undertaking are quashed, possession may be restored as directed by the court overseeing related proceedings when the petitioner does not represent all co-owners, while a claim for compensation may be pursued in a civil court.
material_facts: The petitioner was one of sixteen partners and did not bring the petition on behalf of all partners or join them in a claim for delivery of possession.
The government had taken possession of the partnership’s properties under the invalid orders.
The petitioner alleged that assets had been dissipated and liabilities incurred under the controller’s management.
issues.conclusion: The respondents were to deliver possession to such person or persons as the High Court in the pending appeal directed; the petitioner remained at liberty to pursue a claim for damages by way of compensation in an appropriate civil court.
issues.legal_principle: Where the petitioner does not represent all persons entitled to possession, the Court may direct that possession be delivered to persons designated by the court overseeing related proceedings. A claim for compensation for property or assets lost under the invalid orders may be pursued in an appropriate civil court. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.writ_petition_challenged_property_takeov: A person brought a writ petition challenging a government takeover of property.
predicates.petitioner_did_not_represent_all_coowner: The petitioner did not represent or join all co-owners in seeking delivery of possession.
predicates.properties_were_taken_under_invalid_orde: The government took possession of the properties under orders found invalid.

issues.definition: When a writ challenging a property takeover succeeds but the petitioner does not represent all co-owners, possession is delivered as directed by the related court and compensation may be pursued in civil court.
